title: The landing-lighting mock-up at Foxmere House
public_context: A housing designer writes a technical memo about lighting in a fictional residential building. It uses familiar terms for shared halls, landings, and fixtures, and presents a design topic in ordinary professional prose. The memo and its setting are invented.
source_title: Design memo on the Foxmere House stair landing
source_text:
Foxmere House asked for a lighting mock-up after residents reported that the landing numbers were hard to read from the lower stair. The building's second-floor landing has pale plaster walls, a dark handrail, and two bedroom transoms facing the corridor. We built a full-size corner in an empty first-floor unit using the same wall paint and number plates. The work order called for a clear view of the next step and the room numbers without shining a bare lamp into the transoms.

The first arrangement used one ceiling downlight centered over the landing. From the top step it lit the number plate, but the handrail cast a dark band across the lowest tread when viewed from below. We then tried a wall washer on the corridor side. It evened the plaster and made the number easy to find, though its reflection appeared in both bedroom transoms when the room lights were off.

For the third arrangement, the electrician placed shielded step lights beneath the handrail and a small directional marker beside the number plate. Two design staff walked the stair in both directions while one person watched from the mock bedroom. The lower steps stayed visible from either approach, and the marker could be read without a bright patch on the transom. The step lights did not make the upper landing number readable by themselves; the directional marker supplied that separate task. The same paint sample stayed beside the plate during each pass, so its contrast could be checked against the wall under each fixture.

The housing committee chose the third arrangement for the drawing set, subject to an electrician's review of the existing circuit. It did not approve the decorative pendant shown in the first sketch. No resident took part in the late-night mock-up, and no emergency-power test was included in the work order. The designer therefore kept the drawing marked “for review,” rather than calling it an installed solution.

At the end of the walk-through, the electrician left a note asking for a separate line item for the marker before pricing. I folded the marked plan around the paint sample and left both with the building manager for the next committee meeting.
